vignette:
A 70-year-old woman sits in the chair across from me, her posture rigid, her hands clasped tightly in her lap. She is a widow, a retired hotel manager, and she has not spoken of what happened to her in over forty years. She tells me she is here because her daughter insisted, after finding her on the floor of the bathroom, unable to move, her breath coming in short, sharp gasps.

It began on a Tuesday afternoon in the autumn of 1983. She was 28, the night manager of a mid-sized hotel in a city that prided itself on order and civility. A guest had complained of a disturbance in the parking lot, and she went out to investigate, clipboard in hand. She saw a group of young men, students, she thought, being pushed against a police car. She didn't know them. She didn't know what they had done. She only remembers the sound of a radio crackling, the smell of exhaust and damp asphalt, and then a hand on her shoulder, spinning her around.

She does not remember the words that were exchanged. She remembers the flash of a badge, the cold, hard feeling of the brick wall against her cheek, the pressure of a knee in the small of her back. She remembers the grinding of gravel under her palms as she was forced to the ground. She remembers the weight of a boot on her wrist, pressing down until she felt the bones grind. She remembers the humiliated, silent tears that soaked into the concrete. She was released without a charge, without an apology, told to go back inside and mind her own business.

She went back inside. She finished her shift. She never told anyone. Not her husband, not her mother. She told herself it was a mistake, a misunderstanding, a bad moment in an otherwise good city. She told herself she was strong. She locked the memory in a room in her mind and threw away the key.

For forty years, she kept it locked away. She rose through the ranks of the hotel, becoming the general manager. She was known for her composure, her unflappable calm under pressure. She could handle a fire alarm, a medical emergency, a disgruntled celebrity, all with the same quiet, efficient grace. She was a master of control. She ran her hotel, and she ran her life, with a meticulous, unyielding precision.

Then, six months ago, her husband died. He was the only person who had ever seen her cry, and even then, she had kept the tears silent. With his death, the lock on that old room began to rust. Now, she cannot sleep. She lies in the dark of her empty apartment, and she hears the gravel. She feels the pressure on her wrist. The memory is no longer a distant photograph; it is a live wire, humming under her skin.

She has stopped driving. A police car in her rearview mirror sends her into a cold sweat, her knuckles white on the steering wheel. She will cross the street to avoid a uniformed officer. Last week, a neighbor's door slammed, and she was on the floor of her kitchen before she knew what had happened, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. She avoids the old part of town. She avoids crowds. She avoids anything that feels like a confrontation.

Her daughter, a social worker, found her last month in that bathroom, curled in the fetal position, her breath a ragged, staccato rhythm. She was not having a heart attack. She was not having a stroke. She was 28 years old again, on the cold, wet ground, with a boot on her wrist. She is here now, in my office, because she can no longer keep the door locked. She is terrified of what she will find inside that room. She is terrified of the woman who was once so strong, now brought low by a Tuesday afternoon forty years ago. She tells me she wants to be put back together. She does not yet know that the first step is to let the pieces fall.
